question: A 55-year-old diabetic man presents with rapidly spreading erythema of the left thigh, disproportionate pain, crepitus on palpation, and haemodynamic instability. What is the most appropriate immediate management?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cloxacillin covers only Gram-positive cocci and is inadequate for the polymicrobial coverage required in necrotising fasciitis; surgical debridement is mandatory and must not be delayed.

answers.text: Urgent surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., piperacillin-tazobactam + clindamycin + metronidazole)

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Necrotising fasciitis requires immediate surgical debridement (the cornerstone of treatment) combined with broad-spectrum antibiotics covering Gram-positives, Gram-negatives, and anaerobes. Delay in surgery significantly increases mortality.

answers.text: High-dose oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and outpatient review in 24 hours

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency with mortality approaching 100% if not debrided; outpatient management is never appropriate.

answers.text: IV vancomycin alone pending MRSA culture results

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Vancomycin alone covers MRSA but not the Gram-negative and anaerobic co-pathogens typical of polymicrobial type I necrotising fasciitis, and surgical debridement remains the definitive intervention.

overallFeedback.feedback: Necrotising fasciitis demands immediate surgical debridement plus broad-spectrum antibiotics covering aerobic Gram-positives, Gram-negatives, and anaerobes. Delayed surgery is the leading cause of preventable death.

Excellent. The LRINEC score (≥6 = high risk) can assist diagnosis, but when clinical suspicion is high, surgery must not wait for scoring tools. The 'do not let the skin fool you' pearl applies — overlying skin may look deceptively benign early.
